blocks.text: 1. Audio Models

blocks.alt: A waveform becomes a spectrogram fed into an audio model

blocks.text: Video Models' own closing recap, already covered in Video Models, pointed forward here. Audio Models, extending this course's reach into yet another data modality, bring sound into the same general framework.
They genuinely convert raw sound waves into representations a neural network can actually process, a challenge explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Recapping Discrete Tokens
This connects back to tokenization, already covered generally in Tokenization. Text genuinely arrives as naturally discrete units: words, subwords, or characters.
Raw audio genuinely arrives as a continuous, analog waveform instead, with no built-in discrete boundaries at all, a genuinely fundamental difference explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 3. From Waveform To Spectrogram

blocks.alt: A raw waveform goes through a Fourier transform to produce a spectrogram

blocks.text: This connects back to recapping discrete tokens, already covered in this topic. A genuinely common first step converts the raw waveform into a spectrogram, a genuinely visual representation of sound.
This genuinely shows how much energy exists at each frequency, at each point in time, the exact core transformation explored throughout the rest of this topic.
4. Spectrograms As Images

blocks.alt: A spectrogram is treated like an image

blocks.text: This connects back to from waveform to spectrogram, already covered in this topic. A spectrogram genuinely looks and behaves much like an image: a genuinely two-dimensional grid of values.

This genuinely lets CNN techniques, already covered generally in Convolutional Neural Networks, apply directly to audio, a genuinely elegant reuse of already-familiar tools explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This image-like structure, already covered in this topic, directly explains why many audio classification systems genuinely borrow architectures already covered generally in CNN Architectures, applied to spectrograms instead of photographs.

blocks.text: 5. Audio As A Sequence Over Time

blocks.alt: Time step 1, 2, and 3 form an audio sequence

blocks.text: This connects back to spectrograms as images, already covered in this topic. Audio genuinely also has a natural sequential structure, unfolding moment by moment over time.
This genuinely lets sequence models, already covered generally in Sequence Models, apply directly as well, a genuinely complementary framing explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Audio Tokenization

blocks.alt: An audio signal becomes discrete audio tokens

blocks.text: This connects back to audio as a sequence over time, already covered in this topic. Modern audio models often genuinely learn to discretize continuous audio into audio tokens.

This genuinely mirrors the discrete token idea already covered generally in Tokenization, but learned rather than rule-based, a genuinely modern bridge back to the text-based tokenization already familiar from this course.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This learned discretization, already covered in this topic, directly explains why some modern audio systems can genuinely reuse transformer architectures, already covered generally in Transformers, originally designed for discrete text tokens.

blocks.text: 7. Self Supervised Audio Pretraining

blocks.alt: Unlabeled audio goes through a self-supervised task to produce an audio representation

blocks.text: This connects back to audio tokenization, already covered in this topic. Genuinely just like text pretraining, already covered generally in Transfer Learning, audio models genuinely pretrain on massive amounts of unlabeled sound.
This genuinely learns general audio structure before any task-specific fine-tuning happens, a genuinely direct parallel to the text pretraining already covered generally in this course.
8. Audio Classification Versus Generation

This connects back to self-supervised audio pretraining, already covered in this topic. Genuinely some audio models classify or transcribe existing sound, already covered generally as discriminative tasks across this course.
Genuinely other audio models generate entirely new sound instead, already covered generally in Generative Models, a genuinely useful two-way split explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why Audio Needs Its Own Genuinely Dedicated Representation

blocks.alt: Working with sound data points toward using a dedicated audio representation

blocks.text: This connects back to recapping discrete tokens, already covered in this topic. Audio models, already covered in this topic, genuinely handle the continuous, waveform nature of sound.
This connects back to speech specifically needing its own genuinely dedicated treatment. Speech Models, covered as the next topic in this module, genuinely focus on that specific, important case.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simplified conversion from a raw waveform into a spectrogram-like frequency representation, already covered in this topic.

code.content:
import math
import random
random.seed(0)

def generate_waveform(num_samples=16):
    # already covered as a raw, continuous waveform in this topic
    return [round(math.sin(i * 0.5) + random.uniform(-0.1, 0.1), 3) for i in range(num_samples)]

def simple_spectrogram(waveform, window_size=4):
    # already covered as from waveform to spectrogram in this topic
    spectrogram = []
    for i in range(0, len(waveform) - window_size + 1, window_size):
        window = waveform[i:i + window_size]
        energy = round(sum(abs(v) for v in window) / len(window), 3)
        spectrogram.append(energy)
    return spectrogram

waveform = generate_waveform()
print(f"Raw waveform samples (already covered in this topic): {waveform}")

spectrogram = simple_spectrogram(waveform)
print(f"\nSimplified spectrogram, energy per time window (already covered in this topic): {spectrogram}")
print("\nThis 1D energy sequence stands in for the genuinely 2D time-frequency grid a real spectrogram produces")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Audio models convert raw sound waves into representations a neural network can process.
Text arrives as naturally discrete units; raw audio arrives as a continuous, analog waveform.
A common first step converts the waveform into a spectrogram, a visual representation of sound.
Spectrograms look like images, letting CNN techniques apply directly to audio.
Audio also has a natural sequential structure, letting sequence models apply as well.
Modern audio models often learn to discretize continuous audio into audio tokens.
Audio models pretrain on massive unlabeled sound, similar to text pretraining.
Some audio models classify or transcribe sound; others generate entirely new sound.
Next up: Speech Models, focusing on the specific, important case of spoken language.
